sections.html:
Easley lies mostly in Pickens County, with a small slice in Anderson County, roughly 12 miles west of central Greenville. Population rose from 19,993 in 2010 to 22,921 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 27,319. That is steady growth for a compact city of about 13 square miles.

Because the city straddles a county line, the parcel number and tax notice tell you which assessor and treasurer to call. The town grew up around the railroad and textile mills, so houses come in many ages. Ask an inspector early about wiring, plumbing and roof age, since that is where older houses surprise buyers.

Easley requires a building permit for any structure of 200 square feet or more, and for work of any size that involves plumbing or electrical. The city's FAQ covers what sellers run into most:

  • A remodel needs a permit if it alters the structure or involves electrical, plumbing or mechanical work.
  • Detached structures are capped at 800 square feet and 15 feet in height.
  • Front-yard fences top out at 4 feet and need Public Works approval at 864-855-7916.
  • No one should occupy a home before a Certificate of Occupancy is issued.
  • Any vehicle stored on a property must sit under a factory-made car cover.

Planning and Development handles zoning and permit applications at Easley City Hall, 205 North First Street, phone (864) 855-7908. Code Enforcement is a separate department. The city's FAQ page has more. If you have unpermitted work, ask the city about it before a buyer's inspector finds it.

Depending on the street, a house may be served by Easley Combined Utilities, Blue Ridge Electric Cooperative or the Fort Hill Natural Gas Authority. Look at your bills to see which ones are yours. Moving service is usually easy and rarely takes more than a phone call, but get a final read date from each provider so the closing statement is accurate.

sections.h2: How a property tax appeal works in Pickens County
sections.html:
Pickens County reappraises all property every five years, and an appeal must be filed within 90 days of the notice date. Between reappraisals, values hold for four years unless a sale, new improvement, exemption change or successful appeal alters them. Ask the assessor which cycle your house is in.

Owner-occupied homes are assessed at 4 percent and other property at 6 percent. You can file for the owner-occupied rate any time before the January 15 penalty date. If you stop qualifying and fail to report it, a penalty of 100 percent of the tax can apply. The County Board of Assessment Appeals hears disputes, and the Pickens County Assessor FAQ explains the steps.

OfficeHandlesPhone
AssessorReal property(864) 898-5872

Delinquent tax officeDelinquent taxes(864) 898-5890

After a sale, the owner on December 31 is liable for that year's tax, though the new owner should get the bill. Settle the split on the closing statement.

sections.h2: How the county sets the value
sections.html:
The Assessor uses three approaches. The market approach, built on recent comparable sales, is the main one for houses. The cost approach subtracts depreciation from replacement cost and adds land. The income approach is for property that earns rent. Residential values come from mass appraisal, with statistical models of arm's-length sales.

Square footage comes from exterior measurements, which can differ from a builder's or agent's figures. If your listing sheet and the county record disagree, fix it before a buyer spots it.

The Auditor usually mails real property bills in September. The tax equals taxable value times the assessment rate times the mill levy divided by 1,000. Local taxing bodies set the levy, not the Assessor, so a bill can rise even when the assessment does not. If your mortgage company pays the taxes, forward any bill you receive to them.

A new business or relocation needs a city business license through the Business License Department at City Hall, and an inspection must pass first. A buyer who wants to run a business from the house should check that, plus zoning, in the Unified Development Ordinance.

Planning and Development manages the ordinance and the zoning map, and takes applications for rezoning, annexation, variances and zoning clearance. If you have an unusual lot, a detached building or a home business, request a zoning clearance before you list.

Before a buyer ever walks through, line up the papers that Easley buyers ask about. Start with your parcel number and tax bill, so you know the county and the amount. Pull any permit records for remodels, additions or detached buildings, and the Certificate of Occupancy if one was issued. Find the closing papers from your own purchase if you have them, along with warranties on the roof, HVAC or water heater.

Then walk the property with the city's rules in mind. A shed or garage near the 800 square foot limit, a tall fence or a covered-car rule that was never followed are small things, but a buyer's inspector may flag them. Fixing a fence height costs far less than a stalled closing. If a repair involves electrical or plumbing work, hire someone who will pull the permit, because unpermitted work can turn into a price cut late in the process.

Finally, think about timing. A house listed in spring may draw the most showings, but the date you want to close matters more than the season if you have a move, a job change or a payment deadline. Cash buyers can often close on the schedule you set, which is useful when the date is firm. If the Pickens County or Anderson County tax office has a question about your parcel, a quick call before you sign saves a surprise on the settlement statement.

An Easley seller can list with an agent, sell directly or accept a cash offer. A cash sale tends to fit houses that need permits, repairs or a fast close, because the buyer takes the house as it is and does not wait on a lender.

Gather your payoff figure, your tax bill and any permit records first, then compare the routes. A typical sale moves from contract to inspection to title work, then to closing, where the attorney pays off your loan and settles the tax split. Bring a photo ID and the keys. If a permit is still open, resolve it before the closing date, since an open permit can stall the title work.

faqs.q: What county is Easley, SC, in?
faqs.a: Mostly Pickens County, with a small part in Anderson County. Which assessor and treasurer you use depends on the county your parcel is in.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Pickens County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 90 days from the notice date, and filing does not delay your payment deadline. Attach comparable sales, appraisals or repair estimates to support your number.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair my Easley house before selling?
faqs.a: Yes, for structural changes, for any plumbing, electrical or mechanical work, and for structures of 200 square feet or more. Call Planning and Development at (864) 855-7908 before you start.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax when an Easley house sells mid-year?
faqs.a: The owner on December 31 is liable for that year's tax, though the new owner should get the bill. The closing statement usually divides it between buyer and seller.
The city points to Easley Combined Utilities, Blue Ridge Electric Cooperative and Fort Hill Natural Gas Authority. Your bills show which ones apply to your house.
